title: Complete in Christ: Freedom from Empty Rules
summary: Paul tells the Colossians how hard he labors for churches he has never seen and urges them to continue in Christ as they received him. In Christ all the fullness of God dwells bodily, and in him they have been circumcised, buried and raised in baptism, forgiven, and freed from the powers he disarmed at the cross. So they must not let anyone judge them over food, festivals, and Sabbaths, or disqualify them with visions, angel worship, and harsh rules that only look like wisdom.
story: Chapter 1 set out who Christ is: the image of God, the creator and sustainer of all things, and the reconciler through the cross. Chapter 2 draws the consequence. If Christ is all that, the believer who has him lacks nothing, and any teaching that offers something more than Christ in fact offers less. This is where the letter names the danger that has been in view from the start: a teaching, attractive and apparently wise, that would add rules, rituals, and experiences to faith in Christ. The chapter prepares for the next, where Paul will say what life raised with Christ really looks like.
historical:
The exact shape of the teaching Paul opposes is one of the great puzzles of New Testament study, because he only alludes to it. The clues are here: philosophy and human tradition (verse 8), the spiritual forces or elemental principles of the world (verses 8 and 20), circumcision (verse 11), food and drink, festivals, new moons, and Sabbaths (verse 16), false humility, the worship of angels, and visions (verse 18), and severe rules about handling, tasting, and touching (verses 21 to 23).

Scholars have reconstructed it in several ways. Some, following J. B. Lightfoot in the nineteenth century, see a Jewish movement mixed with early Gnostic ideas about spiritual knowledge and the body. Others see a Jewish mysticism in which fasting and self-denial prepared a person for visions of heaven and participation in the worship offered by angels. Others, including Clinton Arnold, see a local folk religion blending Jewish, pagan, and Christian elements, in which angels were called on for protection from hostile powers. Still others doubt there was a single organized teaching and read Paul as guarding against pressures from the surrounding Jewish and pagan world. The Jewish calendar and food laws are clearly part of it, and so is a concern with spiritual powers; how they fit together remains debated.
cultural:
Philosophy in the ancient world meant more than academic argument; it was a way of life offering wisdom about the gods, the soul, and how to live, and various religious groups presented themselves as philosophies. The phrase translated spiritual forces of the world (stoicheia) could mean the basic elements of the physical world (earth, water, air, fire), the elementary principles of a subject, or the spirits thought to rule the elements and the heavenly bodies. Many people believed these powers governed fate and had to be appeased by rituals and taboos.

The Jewish practices mentioned were real markers of identity that set Jews apart from their neighbors: circumcision, food laws, annual feasts, the monthly new moon celebration, and the weekly Sabbath. Paul does not call them evil. He calls them a shadow of the things to come (verse 17), cast by a reality that has now arrived in Christ. The image in verse 14 is drawn from ordinary business: a cheirographon was a handwritten certificate of debt, signed by the debtor. Nailing it to the cross may echo the Roman practice of posting a notice of a condemned man's crime on his cross (as with Jesus in John 19:19). Verse 15 uses the image of a Roman triumph, the victory parade in which a conquering general led captured enemies through the streets for public display.
literary: The chapter is argument, with a warning at each turn. Verses 1 to 5 are personal: Paul's struggle for the church and his joy at their order and faith. Verses 6 and 7 state the thesis: continue to walk in Christ as you received him. Verse 8 gives the first warning, and verses 9 to 15 give its basis in a dense series of statements about what believers already have in Christ: fullness, circumcision, burial and resurrection, new life, forgiveness, and victory over the powers. Then three warnings follow, each beginning with a form of let no one or why: do not be judged over food and days (verses 16 and 17), do not be disqualified by visions and angel worship (verses 18 and 19), and do not submit to rules about touching and tasting (verses 20 to 23). The images pile up: roots, building, fullness, circumcision, burial, resurrection, a canceled debt, a triumphal parade, a shadow and its body, and a body growing from its head.

outline.t: Paul's struggle for churches he has not seen
Beware empty philosophy; you are complete in Christ
Circumcised, buried, raised, forgiven, and freed
Do not be judged or disqualified

doctrines.note: “For in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form” (verse 9). Christ is not one spiritual power among many, or a first step toward something higher; he is God in bodily form and head over every ruler and authority.

At the cross God forgave all our trespasses, canceled the record of debt that stood against us, and disarmed the hostile powers, making a public spectacle of them (verses 13 to 15). The cross is both payment of a debt and victory over enemies.

Paul connects baptism with union with Christ in his burial and resurrection (verse 12), and relates it to circumcision, which he calls a circumcision not done by hands (verse 11). Christians differ over how closely to link the two: some see baptism as the new covenant sign parallel to circumcision and so baptize infants, while others note that verse 12 speaks of being raised through faith and so baptize believers.

words.note: Stoicheion, element or principle. The word meant the basic parts of something, like letters of the alphabet, the physical elements, or the rudiments of a teaching. By Paul's time it could also refer to spirits associated with the elements and the stars. The BSB translates spiritual forces of the world; other versions give elemental spirits or basic principles. Paul uses the same word in Galatians 4:3 and 9 for the religious bondage of both Jews and Gentiles before Christ.

Cheirographon, a handwritten document, especially a signed certificate of debt. It is the record of our obligation to God, with its decrees that stood against us. God did not merely lower the debt; he wiped it out and nailed it to the cross, where Christ's death settled it.

Thriambeuo, to lead in a triumphal procession. The Roman triumph was a spectacle in which a victorious general paraded his captives through Rome. Paul pictures the cross, which looked like Christ's defeat, as the moment when the hostile powers were stripped and displayed as conquered.

christ: Christ is the sum of everything the Colossians were tempted to seek elsewhere. In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (verse 3), so no secret philosophy can add to him. In him all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily (verse 9), so no angelic mediator is needed. He is the head over every ruler and authority (verse 10), and he defeated them at the cross (verse 15), so no power can claim the believer. The Jewish festivals and Sabbaths were a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ (verse 17). The believer's union with Christ is complete: buried with him, raised with him, made alive with him, and forgiven. The chapter's whole message is that Christ is enough.

hard.q: Does verse 16 mean Christians should not keep the Sabbath or observe special days?
hard.a: Paul says no one should judge believers with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath, because these are a shadow of what was to come. Christians have read this in several ways. Many conclude that the Sabbath law as given to Israel is fulfilled in Christ, who gives the true rest (compare Hebrews 4), so believers are free to observe days or not, as Paul says in Romans 14:5-6; many in this group still see the Lord's Day, Sunday, as a fitting day of worship and rest. Others, in the Reformed and Puritan traditions, hold that the Sabbath principle of one day in seven is a creation ordinance continuing in the Christian Sunday, and that Paul here refers to the ceremonial feasts and the Jewish Sabbath's particular rules. Seventh-day Sabbatarians read the verse as concerning ceremonial sabbaths or the ascetic rules of the false teachers, not the weekly Sabbath of the Ten Commandments. The clearest point is Paul's: observance of days must never be treated as the ground of one's standing before God or a test to judge others by.

questions: Paul warns about teaching that sounds wise and spiritual but draws people away from Christ. What forms does that take today?
Which picture of the cross in verses 13 to 15 (forgiveness, a canceled debt, a victory parade) speaks most to you, and why?
Why do you think strict rules and self-denial can feel so spiritual, and why does Paul say they fail against the indulgence of the flesh?
